paras: The Columbia circus lynching attempt took place on the night of May 11, 1903, at a circus in Columbia, Missouri, when a mob of University of Missouri students tried to seize a Black circus employee to hang him from the tent's center pole. The employee, accused of striking a student, escaped under the tent and was not found. Newspapers across the country carried the story under headlines such as 'Race Riot at a Circus', while Columbia's Black weekly blamed the students for the trouble.

According to a dispatch to the Chicago Chronicle, during a rush for seats the employee struck Stanley Sisson, a student from Toledo, Ohio, on the head with a tent pole, causing 'a dangerous but not fatal wound'. Seeing the blood, students rushed over the ropes, and a member of the football team hit the employee on the chin with his fist. The employee rolled under the tent and escaped in the darkness.

The students then assaulted a number of circus employees and demanded that the man be given up so that they might 'string him to the center pole', but he could not be found. A shorter brief printed in Missouri quoted their cry as 'Lynch the nigger!'. The circus was allowed to go on, but when a Black singer appeared in the concert the performance broke up in 'groans and hisses'. A separate Columbia brief added that the students broke up the circus and that 'a rough house prevailed throughout the town during the night'.

The day after, Sisson was reported to be in serious condition, though a later brief said he was 'not much hurt'. No report of arrests, of any action by the university or the town, or of the employee's fate appears in the coverage. In Columbia, the Black weekly Professional World wrote that the students 'learned a lesson' when they 'tried to take charge of the Pan-American circus and came back with bruised heads and spoiled faces', and argued that a show that paid its license 'should be permitted to do so unmolested'.

The Chronicle dispatch spread quickly, appearing on May 12 and 13 in papers from Washington and New England to Salt Lake City, Oregon, Kentucky and Mississippi. Every version took the employee's blow as fact, but headline writers divided the blame differently: the Washington Evening Star called it a 'Race Riot at a Circus' 'Started by Negro Employee Assaulting College Student', while the Barre Daily Times wrote of 'Lynchers at a Circus' and a 'Wild Band of Students'. The Hattiesburg Daily Progress called the students' demand 'candid', the Morning Astorian headed the story 'Try to Lynch Coon', and a German-language Baltimore paper, placing the scene in South Carolina, mocked the rowdy students who 'only wanted to lynch a negro'.

A week later Missouri country weeklies ran a lighter item, 'College Boys at a Circus', which said the employee had struck a student with a club 'in trying to prevent a jam' and ended with the student 'not much hurt'. The same brief had already appeared without comment in the Black Palladium on May 16, and the Baltimore Afro-American's news digest repeated in one line that the students had tried to lynch an employee 'who had assaulted one of their number'.

The Black reports from Columbia itself told a different story. A correspondent's letter to the Topeka Western World said nothing of a blow and reported only that 'the white students' broke up the show 'when the colored singers appeared on the platform'. The Professional World likewise cast the students as the aggressors and the circus people as the ones who got the better of the fight, warning that 'the college spirit' would 'not always work'.

Accounts differ on the weapon, which the dispatches call a tent pole or a tent peg and the later brief a club. They also differ on the student's injury, from 'dangerous' and 'serious' in the first reports to 'not much hurt' a week later. The story of the first blow comes only from the students' side, while the two Columbia Black reports make the students the aggressors and do not mention it.

bases: A mob of university students tried to seize a Black circus employee to hang him from the tent's center pole and he escaped, an attempted lynching (A1, A5, A11, A19).
No one was killed: the employee escaped (A1, A17); the students' mob acted without authority and over his alleged blow to a student (A1, A5), so this is an attempted lynching, not a completed one.

The Chicago Chronicle dispatch (A1, A5), a separate Columbia brief (A11), the 'College Boys' brief (A17, A19) and two Black-press reports, one from Columbia itself (A15, A16), agree that students broke up a circus and went after a Black employee, though they differ on details.

accounts.label: Chicago Chronicle dispatch
accounts.gist: During a rush for seats the employee struck Sisson with a tent pole, causing a dangerous wound; students chased him, demanded him from the employees to string him to the center pole, and broke up the concert when a Black singer appeared.

accounts.label: Separate Columbia brief
accounts.gist: Sisson was in serious condition; the students broke up the circus demanding the employee, whom they 'started to lynch', and a rough house went on through the night.

accounts.label: 'College Boys at a Circus' brief
accounts.gist: The employee struck a student with a club 'in trying to prevent a jam'; students cried 'Lynch the nigger!' and he escaped; the student was not much hurt.

accounts.label: Black correspondent at Columbia
accounts.gist: White university students broke up a large circus when the colored singers appeared, with no mention of a blow or a lynching threat.

accounts.label: Professional World editorial
accounts.gist: Students tried to take charge of the circus and came back with bruised heads and spoiled faces; a licensed show should be left unmolested.

framing.detail: The Evening Star headed it 'Race Riot at a Circus. Started by Negro Employee Assaulting College Student', while other headlines put the students first ('Lynchers at a Circus', 'Students on Rampage'); the text everywhere took the employee's blow as fact.
Hattiesburg called the students' demand 'candid' and Astoria headed it 'Try to Lynch Coon'; a Baltimore German paper mocked the 'rowdy sons of the Muses' who 'only wanted to lynch a negro'.
Missouri country weeklies ran a light 'College Boys at a Circus' item quoting the cry 'Lynch the nigger!' and noting the student was 'not much hurt'.

Columbia's Professional World said the students 'learned a lesson' and that licensed exhibitors should be left unmolested; the Western World's Columbia letter blamed the white students for breaking up the show.
The Palladium reprinted the 'College Boys' brief without comment and the Afro-American's digest repeated that the employee 'had assaulted one of their number'.

conflicts.note: All versions come from the students' side of the story; no account from the employee appears.
The first-day dispatches describe a serious wound; the later brief says the student was not much hurt. No follow-up on his condition was found.
